title: Bob’s Burgers Dialogue
text:
This TidyTuesday dataset from November 19, 2024 contains diologue data from the show Bob’s Burgers.

library(ggplot2)

  episodes <- read.csv("episode_metrics.csv")

  ggplot(episodes, aes(x = season, y = avg_length, group = season)) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "blue")+
    labs(
      title = "Dialogue Length Per Bob's Burgers Seasons",
      x = "Seasons",
      y= "Average Characters Per Line"
    
    )








In this plot that compares average diologue lengths among several seasons of Bob’s Burgers each episode contributes one value: its average number of characters per line of diologue. Within the box plot, each line in the middle of the box represents the median. A higher median indicates a longer diologue and vice versa. Boxas that are taller indicate a greater variation of diologue length within a season, and shorter boxes indicate the opposite.
Sources:
R for Data Science. TidyTuesday: Bob’s Burgers Episodes. November 19, 2024. https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2024/2024-11-19/readme.md
Ponce, Steven. bobsburgersR: Collection of datasets from the Bob’s Burgers animated sitcom. Original transcript dataset. https://github.com/poncest/bobsburgersR

title: Steam Video Game Popularity
text:
A TidyTuesday dataset from March 16, 2021 that contains monthly player activity for games on Steam.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

games <- read.csv("games.csv")

games_select <- filter(
  games,
  year == 2021,
  month == "January",
  gamename == "Apex Legends" |
    gamename == "Rust" |
    gamename == "Rocket League" |
   gamename == "Dota 2" |
    gamename == "Team Fortress 2" |
    gamename == "Counter-Strike: Global Offensive"
)

ggplot(games_select, aes(x = gamename, y = avg)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Player Activity on Steam in January 2021",
    x = "Game",
    y = "Average Players"
  ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








This bar chart compares the average concurrent players for six steam games in January 2021 (Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Dota 2, Team Fortress 2, Rust, Apex Legends, and Rocket League). Counter-Strike: Global Offensive had the highest average of 743,210 concurrent players, followed by Dota 2 with 432,672. Rust averaged 142,117 players while Team Fortress 2, Apex Legends, and Rocket League all had fewer than 100,000 concurrent active players. These results convey a large difference in activity between games withinn the month of January 2021.
Sources:
R for Data Science. (2021, March 16). TidyTuesday: Video Games and Sliced. Dataset and documentation.
michau96. (n.d.). Popularity of games on Steam [Dataset]. Kaggle. Kaggle dataset.

title: “Exploring Netflix Titles” author: “Alex Erickson” format: html execute: warning: false message: false
How do Netflix story themes differ by country and between movies and TV shows?

library(tidyverse)

netflix <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv"
)

Rows: 7787 Columns: 12
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (11): show_id, type, title, director, cast, country, date_added, rating,...
dbl  (1): release_year

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

netflix_countries <- netflix |>
  filter(
    country == "United States" |
    country == "India" |
    country == "United Kingdom" |
    country == "Japan" |
    country == "South Korea" |
    country == "Canada"
  )

netflix_countries |>
  count(country, type)

# A tibble: 12 × 3
   country        type        n
   <chr>          <chr>   <int>
 1 Canada         Movie     118
 2 Canada         TV Show    59
 3 India          Movie     852
 4 India          TV Show    71
 5 Japan          Movie      69
 6 Japan          TV Show   157
 7 South Korea    Movie      36
 8 South Korea    TV Show   147
 9 United Kingdom Movie     193
10 United Kingdom TV Show   204
11 United States  Movie    1850
12 United States  TV Show   705



netflix_themes <- netflix_countries |>
  filter(!is.na(description)) |>
  mutate(description_c = str_to_lower(description))

netflix_themes |>
  select(title, description_c)

# A tibble: 4,461 × 2
   title              description_c                                             
   <chr>              <chr>                                                     
 1 9                  in a postapocalyptic world, rag-doll robots hide in fear …
 2 21                 a brilliant group of students become card-counting expert…
 3 187                after one of his high school students attacks him, dedica…
 4 706                when a doctor goes missing, his psychiatrist wife treats …
 5 1920               an architect and his wife move into a castle that is slat…
 6 1922               a farmer pens a confession admitting to his wife's murder…
 7 3022               stranded when the earth is suddenly destroyed in a myster…
 8 15-Aug             on india's independence day, a zany mishap in a mumbai ch…
 9 '89                mixing old footage with interviews, this is the story of …
10 ​​Kuch Bheege Alfaaz after accidentally connecting over the internet, two stra…
# ℹ 4,451 more rows

netflix_themes <- netflix_themes |>
mutate(
    family = str_detect(
      description_c,
      "\\b(family|families|mother|father|siblings?)\\b"
    ),
    romance = str_detect(
      description_c,
      "\\b(romance|romantic|love|relationships?)\\b"
    ),
    crime = str_detect(
      description_c,
      "\\b(murders?|police|detectives?|criminals?)\\b"
    ),
    adventure = str_detect(
      description_c,
      "\\b(adventures?|journeys?|quests?|expeditions?)\\b"
    )
  )

t_summary <- netflix_themes |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    family = mean(family) * 100,
    romance = mean(romance) * 100,
    crime = mean(crime) * 100,
    adventure = mean(adventure) * 100
  )

t_long <- t_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(family, romance, crime, adventure),
    names_to = "theme",
    values_to = "percentage"
  )

ggplot(t_long, aes(x = theme, y = country, fill = percentage)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%"))) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#EFF6FF", high = "#60A5FA") +

    labs(
    title = "Netflix Themes by Country",
    subtitle = "Percentage of descriptions mentioning each theme's keywords",
    x = "Theme",
    y = "Production Country",
    fill = "Titles (%)",
  ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))








The heatmap above sorts Netflix themes by country (United States, India, Unnited Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and Canada) and displays the percentage of descriptions mentioning each themes keywords. Family keywords apear the most in descriptions from India at roughly 18.3%. South Korean descriptions of titles mention romance at 15.8%, while Japan has the highest percentage of adventure mentions at 8.9%. The patterns emphasize that themes vary by country however, this acounts for both tv shows and movies, which will be compared below.

netflix_themes <- netflix_themes |>
  mutate(
    romance_w = str_extract(
      description_c,
      "\\b(romance|romantic|love|relationships?)(?!\\w)"
    ),
    romance = !is.na(romance_w))

romance_sum <- netflix_themes |>
    group_by(country, type) |>
    summarise(percent = mean(romance) * 100, titles = n()) |>
    mutate(type = fct_relevel(type, "Movie", "TV Show"))

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by country and type.
ℹ Output is grouped by country.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(country, type))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

ggplot(romance_sum, aes(x = country, y = percent, fill = type)) +
    geom_col(position = "dodge") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("lightgreen", "darkgreen")) +
    labs(
    title = "Romance Mentions by Country in Movies vs. TV Shows",
    subtitle = "Percentage of descriptions matching romance keywords",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Titles Mentioning Romance (%)",
    fill = "Content Type"
    ) +
    theme( axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))








The boxplot above shows the Romance mentions by country in TV Shows vs Movies. South Korea has the largest difference of romance mentions with romance keywords apearing in the descriptions of 19% of TV Shows but only 3% of movies. India shows the opposite pattern, with romance keyword mentions being about 4% more common in movies then TV shows. This also relates to the heatmap as this data helps show that South Korea’s high pecentage in romance keywords is heaviy driven by romance TV shows.
Sources:
R for Data Science. TidyTuesday: Netflix Shows. April 20, 2021. https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/readme.md
Bansal, Shivam. Netflix Movies and TV Shows. Original dataset, collected from Flixable. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/shivamb/netflix-shows
